(a) $f(-6) = f(-2) + \int_{-2}^{-6} f'(x)\,dx = 7 - \int_{-6}^{-2} f'(x)\,dx = 7 - 4 = 3$

$f(5) = f(-2) + \int_{-2}^{5} f'(x)\,dx = 7 - 2\pi + 3 = 10 - 2\pi$

(b) $f'(x) > 0$ on the intervals $[-6, -2]$ and $(2, 5)$.
Therefore, $f$ is increasing on the intervals $[-6, -2]$ and $[2, 5]$.

(c) The absolute minimum will occur at a critical point where $f'(x) = 0$ or at an endpoint.

$f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = -2, x = 2$

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
| -6 | 3 |
| -2 | 7 |
| 2 | $7 - 2\pi$ |
| 5 | $10 - 2\pi$ |

The absolute minimum value is $f(2) = 7 - 2\pi$.

(d) $f''(-5) = \frac{2 - 0}{-6 - (-2)} = -\frac{1}{2}$

$\lim_{x \to 3^-} \frac{f'(x) - f'(3)}{x - 3} = 2$ and $\lim_{x \to 3^+} \frac{f'(x) - f'(3)}{x - 3} = -1$

$f''(3)$ does not exist because
$$\lim_{x \to 3^-} \frac{f'(x) - f'(3)}{x - 3} \neq \lim_{x \to 3^+} \frac{f'(x) - f'(3)}{x - 3}.$$
